title: AIR-VLA: Vision-Language-Action Systems for Aerial Manipulation
one_liner: A new benchmark and dataset reveals what vision-language-action models can and cannot do when controlling a flying robot with a robotic arm.
lead: Robots that follow language instructions by watching video have worked well when sitting on the ground, but flying robots with arms are harder — they move in three dimensions, the arm and drone interact with each other, and tasks take many steps. This paper builds the first test suite designed specifically for these aerial systems, with simulated examples and real measurements, to show which AI models work and which fail.

problem.h2: Flying robots are not like ground robots
paras: Today's AI systems that understand images and language and decide what actions to take (called vision-language-action models) work well when a robot sits still or rolls on the ground. But flying robots with arms are different: they must balance themselves in mid-air, the arm's movement shakes the drone, and tasks need many steps. Existing models trained on ground robots do not account for these challenges.

A beginner might try using a model trained on ground robots and hope it transfers to the air. But this fails because the model has never seen floating-base dynamics (how a UAV stays stable), never learned about the tight coupling between the arm and the drone (moving the arm changes the drone's stability), and never practiced long-horizon planning (holding a sequence of steps in mind). The mismatch is fundamental.

callout.html: AIR-VLA is a test suite with 3000 simulated examples and metrics tailored to aerial manipulation, revealing which models can handle the unique challenges of flying arms.

steps.text: Creates a physics engine with a flying drone, a robotic arm, and objects to grasp, run through realistic forces.
A human remotely drives the drone+arm 3000 times, performing pick-and-place and multi-step manipulation tasks.

Base manipulation (how well the drone holds position), object understanding (finding things to grasp), semantic reasoning (following language), long-horizon planning (remembering and chaining actions).

steps.b: Runs existing models on the tests
steps.text: Tests large pre-trained models, distilled fast versions, and traditional imitation-learning baselines with identical inputs.

steps.b: Reports what each model can do
steps.text: Shows success rates per task type, exposes weaknesses (e.g. a fast model fails on complex tasks), and measures the gap between what models do on step one versus steps two through five.

paras: This paper does not change the models themselves. Instead, it changes what we measure: it introduces a new test suite and four types of evaluation metrics, each focused on challenges unique to aerial systems.

hidden.name: multi-step performance drop
paras: The paper measures something that ground-robot benchmarks miss: how much worse a model's decisions become on the second, third, and later steps of a task. On the first action, a model predicts correctly much of the time. But once the robot moves and the world changes, the model must update its understanding from the new camera view and remember what it is trying to do. This measurement reveals whether models can handle mental burden across time.

The paper calculates this by running models on tasks with multiple steps, measuring success on the first step separately from steps two-through-five, and comparing the drop. A model that maintains 85% accuracy on step one but falls to 20% on step two has a 65-point degradation. This number is invisible in traditional benchmarks that only report final success or failure.

heat.caption: Darker means more accurate. Dashed box shows the drop: high on step 1, then collapses on later steps.

reads.html: When a robot makes a long sequence of moves, each step depends on seeing the new world created by the previous step. If the model loses track or misreads the new camera view, the entire sequence fails. This drop from step one to steps two-plus is the core measurement.

Table 1 shows task success broken into sub-metrics. For long-horizon tasks, the paper compares initial-subtask success to multi-step success, revealing the degradation patterns and showing that even the best foundation models exhibit notable performance drops after the first step.

mechanism.h2: Why this matters: the real reason long-horizon fails
paras: Vision-language-action models work by reading the current image, the current task instruction, and predicting the next action. On step one, this works well: the camera shows the original scene clearly, and the model has never been wrong yet. But on step two, everything has changed. The robot may have moved, the target may now be partially hidden, and the model must integrate the instruction (still the original language) with this new visual context.

The challenge is twofold. First, the model must track the state of a flying system across time — the drone's position, the arm's joint angles, whether an object is grasped — by reading the camera alone. Ground robots move slowly and predictably in 2D. Aerial systems fly in 3D and the arm can create chaotic forces. Second, the model must remember the intent ('pick up the red box and place it on the table') and revise its understanding as the world evolves. If the model misses a detail on step two (e.g. the box slipped), all remaining steps will fail. This cascading dependency makes long-horizon tasks exponentially harder than one-shot prediction.

The paper reveals this by running the same model on single-step tasks (usually successful) and multi-step tasks (where performance plummets). Because the model code does not change, only the task length changes, the drop is purely a problem of visual understanding and temporal reasoning at scale.

stages.s: Task: 'Grasp the box'. Camera image 1. Model predicts action 1.
Step 1 executes. Drone moves, arm reaches. New camera image 2.
Model reads image 2 and original task. Predicts action 2. Must recover state.
Step 2 executes. Drone oscillates slightly. Image 3 is complex, arm partly out of frame.
Model's action 3 guess becomes unreliable. Error cascades. Task fails.

math.h2: The metric: measuring the drop across steps
math.words: Success rate per step = count of correct actions at step i divided by total attempts at step i. Degradation = success at step 1 minus average success at steps 2 through N.
math.equation: step_success_i = (correct_actions_at_i / total_attempts) * 100, degradation = step_success_1 - mean(step_success_2, ..., step_success_N)
symbols: percentage of correct actions at step i, measured from 100 test runs
how many times the model chose the right action at step i
how many test runs were executed
the difference between step 1 success and average success on remaining steps

worked.title: A tiny worked example
lines: Suppose π0 model runs 10 tasks with 5 steps each.
Step 1: model succeeds on 9 out of 10 tasks. Success rate: 90%.
Step 2: model succeeds on 7 out of 10 tasks. Success rate: 70%.
Step 3: model succeeds on 5 out of 10 tasks. Success rate: 50%.
Step 4: model succeeds on 4 out of 10 tasks. Success rate: 40%.
Step 5: model succeeds on 3 out of 10 tasks. Success rate: 30%.
This large drop signals that the model struggles to maintain performance as the task unfolds.

math.note: The degradation metric isolates the problem of long-horizon reasoning: one model can ace the first move but stumble on the sequence.

charts.title: Imitation learning baseline
charts.note: Baseline models trained only on teleoperated data collapse quickly after the first action.

charts.title: Foundation model (large variant)
charts.note: Pre-trained on massive data from many robot types, this model encounters many examples of recovering from new situations mid-task, so it maintains better performance. Yet it still degrades 23 points by step 2-5 because even large models struggle with the compounding uncertainty of 3D aerial tasks.

charts.title: Foundation model (fast distilled variant)
charts.note: Compressing a large model into a faster version catastrophically breaks long-horizon reasoning in aerial systems because the compressed model must make its memory of the task and world fit into fewer parameters, and those parameters are now forced to serve both recognition and reasoning — ground robots tolerate this trade-off, but 3D aerial tasks require sustained memory across steps.

items.html: When large pre-trained models are compressed to run faster (called distillation), the smaller model forgets how to track the world across steps in 3D space. This happens because the compressed model has fewer parameters to store information about what changed and why, so it cannot maintain a mental picture across multiple actions. This trade-off is acceptable for ground robots (which move in 2D and have simpler state) but catastrophic for aerial systems where every step matters because a lost detail in step 3 ruins steps 4 and 5.

The benchmark includes a test with only onboard and wrist cameras (no global view). Many models rely on the global third-person view to understand where the drone is in space. Removing that view causes sharp performance drops, exposing that models have not learned accurate 3D spatial reasoning.

All examples are in simulation. Real-world air currents, sensor noise, and uneven weight balance may cause additional failures not captured in the test suite. The paper does not test on actual flying robots.

The paper notes that some model predictions cause dangerous interactions with the environment (e.g., crashing into a wall, dropping an object unsafely). Current models do not incorporate constraints that prevent unsafe actions, and the benchmark does not penalize them heavily for safety violations.

A model succeeds by maintaining reasonable performance on steps 2-5 (within 15 points of step 1), passing the no-global-view test with minimal degradation, and predicting actions that respect safety (e.g., never command the arm to rotate beyond joint limits).

demo.h2: What a runnable demo should prove
paras: Build a simulation of a flying drone with a robotic arm. Load a pre-trained vision-language-action model (e.g., a foundation model or OpenVLA). Give the model a language command like 'pick up the blue cylinder and place it in the bin.' Run the model step-by-step for 10 actions. Record whether the model succeeds at each step and compute the step-by-step success rate. Then measure the degradation: how much does performance drop from step 1 to steps 2-10? Run the same task with the fast compressed variant and compare the degradation. A reader should see the foundation model hold up reasonably (85% to 65%), while the compressed variant collapses (70% to 15%).
demo.closing: The demo makes it impossible to miss: foundation models trained on broad robot data handle multi-step aerial tasks better than distilled or ground-only models because they have learned patterns of recovery and spatial reasoning across many embodiments, but all models still struggle to sustain performance beyond the first action in long-horizon sequences because even broad training cannot solve the fundamental problem of accumulating errors in 3D space when the world state is observed only through a camera.
